opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, if I look back at it objectively, I think my PhD output was fine by the standards of that time, but not spectacular. I did my PhD at UC San Diego with Zhuowen Tu, and that was roughly 2013 to 2018, right when deep learning was just taking off in computer vision. The bar back then was quite different. If you had a few solid first-author papers at CVPR or ICCV, and maybe one or two that people actually used, you were considered a strong PhD student. Things like holistically-nested edge detection, the deeply-supervised nets work, and later ResNeXt during my internship at FAIR, those were the projects I'm most associated with from that period.

But I always tell people that a lot of it was timing. The field was much smaller. There was a lot of low-hanging fruit, and if you were reasonably sensitive to where things were going, you could make a contribution that lasted. ResNeXt, for example, is not a very complicated idea. It's about grouped convolutions and this notion of cardinality as another dimension besides depth and width. In today's world, an idea like that might be one experiment in a much larger paper.

When I compare myself to my students today, I genuinely feel that many of them are stronger than I was at the same stage. They're more technically mature, they can handle much larger systems, and they understand the whole stack, from data to infrastructure to training at scale. The volume of papers people publish now is also much higher. Some PhD students have more papers in their first two or three years than I had in my entire PhD.

But I don't think that automatically means their situation is easier or that the comparison is fair in either direction. The field is far more crowded now, and it's much harder to find a problem that is truly yours. Back then, the challenge was more like: can you see the direction early? Now the challenge is: in a world where everyone is chasing the same few directions with huge resources, can you still have taste and find something that matters, rather than just adding a percentage point?

So my honest assessment is that I was a decent student who was lucky to be in the right place at the right time, with a great advisor and great collaborators. And what I try to pass on to my students is not "publish more," but to care about whether a piece of work will still mean something five years later. That standard, I think, hasn't changed between my era and theirs.

r001.rationale: He says the volume of papers is much higher now and that some students publish more in their first two or three years than he did across his PhD.

r002.rationale: He says many students are stronger than he was at the same stage, but describes their skills and technical maturity rather than judging their research work as substantially better than his PhD work.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, if I take my PhD output and put it next to what my students are doing now, it looks very thin. I was at UCSD with Zhuowen Tu, and over five or six years I had maybe a handful of papers I'd actually stand behind. Holistically-nested edge detection, which got a lot of citations. ResNeXt, which was really a Facebook internship project at the end. A couple of others. That was considered a good PhD at the time.

Today a strong student in my group might have that many first-author papers in two years. The volume is just on a different scale. Part of that is tooling. When I started, we were writing Caffe layers in C++ and waiting a week for an ImageNet run. Now you fork a repo, change the architecture, and have a result overnight. The barrier to going from idea to experiment has basically collapsed.

But I try to be careful about what that comparison actually means. The bar for what counts as a contribution has moved too. Back then, if you got two points on a benchmark with a clean idea, that was a paper and people remembered it. Now two points is noise, and the field is so crowded that even a good idea gets rediscovered three times in the same month. So my students work harder and produce more, but it's much harder for any single piece to be the one people cite ten years later.

The thing I keep telling them is that the metric I actually care about isn't the count. When I look back at my own PhD, the papers that mattered weren't the ones I rushed. They were the ones where I spent months being confused about something that seemed basic, like why do we need so many hand-designed stages in edge detection, or why does increasing width work differently from increasing depth. That slow confusion is the part that's hardest to preserve now, because the incentives push you to ship. So I'd say my students are better engineers and better researchers than I was at their stage, by a lot. What I try to protect for them is the permission to be slow sometimes, because that was the luxury my era gave me almost by accident.

r001.rationale: He contrasts his handful of PhD papers over five or six years with current students producing that many first-author papers in two years.

r002.rationale: He says his students are better researchers and engineers than he was at their stage, but does not judge their work as substantially better than his PhD work; he also distinguishes higher output from lasting impact.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate the number of papers from the substance of the work. Looking back at my PhD, I would ask: Did I find a meaningful problem? Did I develop my own judgment? Did I produce something that other people could build on? Those are more useful questions than whether my publication count would look competitive today.

For students now, the pace is much faster, and the pressure to publish is higher. It’s easy to look at their output and then judge your younger self by that standard, but that’s not really a fair comparison. The tools, the resources, and the expectations are different.

At the same time, I don’t think faster output should automatically become a higher requirement. I’d rather a student have a piece of work they can explain deeply—why the problem matters, why their approach makes sense, and what they learned when it failed—than simply accumulate papers. To me, the important outcome of a PhD is becoming an independent researcher. The papers should be evidence of that development.

r001.rationale: The response says publishing pressure and pace are higher today, but does not state that many current students publish far more papers than Xie did during his PhD.

r002.rationale: The response does not judge current students’ work to be substantially better than Xie’s PhD work; it cautions that the eras and expectations differ.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate the quality of the work from the number of papers. If I look back at my PhD by the standards of that time, I’m happy with what I did. But I wouldn’t take that publication record and use it as a checklist for my students today. The field has changed, and the pace is very different.

Students today can build on tools and ideas that we didn’t have, but they also face much more competition and much more noise. Producing more papers doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve developed better judgment. What I care about is whether a student can identify a meaningful problem, explain why it matters, and take ownership of an idea—even when the experiments don’t work.

That’s also how I’d want to judge my own PhD: not just by what came out of it, but by whether I learned how to do research independently.
